dispatches.editorNote: Commissioned for the October 28 Early edition. Source checks made before publication; refresh the current board once at release. No outreach was sent. The public record establishes the stalled score, not its cause. This feature supersedes the older direction to treat Mostik only as background.
dispatches.headline: What happened to Mostik? The early ARC leader still sitting at 7.51

sections.heading: The former leader is still on the board
sections.text:
Mostik arrived in public with a first-place claim, a team of mathematicians and a promise to let AI models exchange more than words. Nearly two months later, the number beside its ARC-AGI-3 entry is still 7.51. The company has continued talking about research. Its public competition score has not kept pace.

The four-letter team was CSTL. On August 31, ARC Prize announced CSTL’s 7.51 high score. On September 2, Sasha Malysheva identified Mostik as the former CSTL team in a reply to that announcement. This is a direct identification by the company’s leader, rather than a match inferred from a name or avatar.

In the live Kaggle board checked for this investigation, mostik.ai was 2,098th at 7.51 with 47 entries and a Last field of roughly two months. The nearby saved collector observation, at 03:47 UTC on October 28, placed the same team, ID 16364346, one rank higher at the same score and entry count. The entry remains listed; it has fallen far down the public standings. These are dated public-board observations, not final private results. At the Early edition’s closing collector observation on October 28 (2026-10-28T09:47:50Z), mostik.ai stood 2,112th at 7.51, with 47 recorded entries.

sections.heading: The milestone was September’s second checkpoint
sections.text:
The launch timing matters. Milestone 1 closed on June 30; ARC Prize published its winners on July 6. Mostik’s September 2 launch therefore came after that award and before Milestone 2’s September 30 deadline. The organizer’s August CSTL announcement itself pointed to September 30 as the next milestone.

Milestone awards rewarded qualifying open-source solutions. They were not a simple reprint of every team’s unrestricted public-board position. On October 1, ARC Prize named Daniel Franzen, Lord Han Solo and Lohit Siriki as the three Milestone 2 winners. Mostik was not among those award recipients. That omission alone tells us neither whether it sought the award nor why its score stopped improving.

The field was already changing in early September. Franzen’s own solution write-up says a model upgrade briefly put him first on September 6 before Tufa overtook him. That supplies a dated account of another contender moving past the earlier leading group; it does not establish the exact moment Mostik lost first place.

sections.heading: The bridge demonstration and the competition recipe
sections.text:
The research pitch was easy to get excited about. Instead of making one model write a message for another to read, Mostik trained a connection between their internal representations. Its published demonstration paired a large GLM-5.2 sender with a much smaller Qwen-3.5 receiver. The sender processed the prompt; the receiver generated the answer. Both underlying models stayed frozen while the connection was trained.

The comparisons need their labels. Malysheva’s launch post advertised results at 80% of frontier-model accuracy with twentyfold faster performance. The company’s technical page describes closing half the accuracy gap between its two models and using 2.5 times less compute than a model matched for score. Those statements compare different things; they cannot be substituted for one another or read as an ARC score.

WIRED reported the company’s early ARC lead but said it withheld the contest details because it wanted to win. The reviewed public material does not establish that the published large-and-small-model demonstration was the exact system behind 7.51. Nor does the leaderboard isolate how much any bridge contributed. A promising demonstration and a reproducible explanation of a competition score remain different pieces of evidence.

sections.heading: Mostik has continued to speak
sections.text:
The company’s visible research activity did not end with the launch. On October 12, Malysheva described an on-site brainstorm with most of the team and said Stas Smirnov had joined it. On October 26, she discussed another group’s latent-communication paper and explained Mostik’s interest in transmitting the computation of a larger model. Neither post announced a new ARC submission or score.

That distinction changes the story. The public record supports a stalled competitive showing alongside continued research commentary. It does not support a claim that Mostik shut down, vanished entirely or announced its withdrawal.

The current Kaggle roster lists eight accounts: avgaydashenko, gatamaz, godjan, korogodsky, malyshevasasha, rolion, tehnar and vitalique. Mostik’s advertised company headcount and a contest roster measure different groups. The company’s larger headcount does not establish that every employee worked on the entry, or that a competition rule was broken.

sections.heading: The missing answer is why
sections.text:
The reviewed sources leave the central question unanswered: why has Mostik not posted a higher public score since the launch period? Its score now matches the figure ARC Prize announced on August 31. That is evidence of no net improvement between those observations, not a complete submission-by-submission history.

A public board cannot reveal private experiments, unsuccessful runs or what a team intends to submit next. The saved collector has a September 6 timestamp beside this entry, but that field is not evidence of when the team last conducted research. This investigation has not established that Mostik abandoned ARC, encountered a particular technical failure, or chose commercial work over the contest. It has also found no substantiated withdrawal or disqualification notice in the sources reviewed.

The useful questions for Mostik are concrete: Is the team still actively contesting ARC-AGI-3? What produced 7.51, and what part did latent bridging play? What prevented a higher public score? Will it release the agent, bridge and enough evaluation detail for others to reproduce the result?

No request for comment was sent for this article. There is no refusal to report. For now, the strongest finding is a gap between a well-publicized early lead and a public competition result that the field has left behind. The cause of that gap remains undisclosed in the material reviewed.

dispatches.editorNote: Special evening feature commissioned by Mark Barney. Reporting refreshed October 28 from the original organizer posts, their public discussion and ARC Prize’s own result and benchmark pages. Broader ARC-1/2 trends lead; both Kaggle races receive separate closing reports.
dispatches.headline: The gaps hiding under ARC-1’s ceiling

image.alt: AI editorial illustration: puzzle-solving robots crowd under an ARC-1 glass ceiling, spread out on an ARC-2 staircase and face an open ARC-3 landscape.
image.caption: Beyond the Ceiling — AI editorial illustration for the October 28 special evening feature. The chambers and staircase are a metaphor for tests revealing different abilities, not a data chart or a forecast.

sections.heading: The gap behind the tie
sections.text:
Two AI systems can get the same mark on ARC-1 and finish more than twenty points apart on ARC-2. That is the striking finding in the comparison ARC Prize published on Wednesday—and the reason Greg Kamradt thinks the older puzzle format still has more to tell us.

The official results give a concrete example. Kimi K3 and GPT-5.4 Pro, at the tested settings, both scored just under 95 percent on ARC-1. On ARC-2, Kimi scored about 60 percent and GPT-5.4 Pro about 83 percent. The first test makes them look evenly matched. The second opens a gap of twenty-three points.

An easier test can run out of room before the systems taking it run out of differences. Once strong models are getting nearly everything right, another good result tells us less about what separates them. ARC-2 gives those differences somewhere to show up.

sections.heading: The pattern matters as much as the gap
sections.text:
There is another side to the story. Across the models ARC Prize compared, good ARC-1 scores generally went with good ARC-2 scores. The points followed a smooth curve. Stronger performance on the older test usually carried over to the harder one.

Those two findings belong together. The tests share a broad pattern, yet the harder one can still separate systems that look tied. Think of an exam that tells you which students are doing well but no longer tells you much about the differences among the best students. A tougher exam can reveal those differences without testing a completely unrelated subject.

ARC-2 also asks more of the solver. Its puzzles can require several rules to work together, a symbol to carry a meaning, or the right rule to change with the situation. Kamradt's point is that this extended the life of the original ARC idea: a small colored grid can still ask a harder question.

This chart does not tell us how fast AI will improve next month. Matt Mazur made that distinction in the discussion: it compares scores across tests. It is not a forecast of progress over time.

sections.heading: Which puzzles are doing the work?
sections.text:
Kamradt's next suggestion is more interesting than another overall ranking. He wants to use the accumulated results to work out how difficult the individual public ARC-1 and ARC-2 puzzles are. Jack Cole raised the problem of top scores bunching together and suggested looking more closely at individual tasks too.

That could turn a league table into a more useful account of what models can and cannot do. Two systems might finish with the same total while solving different puzzles. One might manage a difficult combination of rules that defeats the other. The total would hide that difference; the puzzle-by-puzzle record could expose it.

There is a further question worth asking: which puzzles actually separate the strongest systems? A puzzle almost everyone fails is hard, but it may tell us little about the differences between them. The useful next test needs challenges that reveal something.

These are proposals for further work. Kamradt explicitly said there are no plans for an ARC-2.5 release. The news is the direction of the conversation: better use of the tests and results already in hand.

sections.heading: ARC-3 adds the experience of finding out
sections.text:
ARC-3 takes that search into a different setting. The system has to act, see what happened and learn how an unfamiliar game works. It must discover useful moves and change its approach as it goes, rather than only supply the missing answer to a puzzle.

That gives the people building and testing these systems more to inspect. A final mark tells them how the run ended. The play itself can show whether the system noticed a useful clue, repeated a bad move or learned something it could use later.

ARC Prize also reported a broad link between stronger ARC-2 and ARC-3 results, with exceptions. The interesting thread running through all three tests is how to keep revealing differences as systems improve. ARC-2 makes the puzzles more demanding. ARC-3 lets us watch a system try to find its way through something new.

sections.heading: A higher mark still has a price
sections.text:
For the Kaggle teams, there is a practical reason to care about all this. They need to know which changes make a system more capable, where it still gets stuck and what the improvement costs.

The tied-score example has a useful second detail. The official table lists the GPT-5.4 Pro result at more than ten times Kimi K3's cost per ARC-2 puzzle. The higher score reveals a real difference in the published results, but it is not a comparison at an equal budget. A team working within competition limits has to care about both. These model evaluations are separate from the Kaggle contest standings.

The desk's reading of Wednesday's discussion is that ARC's next useful story may be hiding inside the scores we already have: the puzzles that separate close rivals, the strengths concealed by a shared total, and the point at which a test stops giving us enough room to see.

The aim is to keep asking questions that let a better system show what it can do.
